paras: The attempted lynching of Esau Lovely took place on the night of July 12, 1903, when a crowd of 200 to 400 men gathered at the St. Mary Parish jail in Franklin, Louisiana, to lynch Lovely, a Black prisoner accused of robbing a white woman that morning. U.S. Senator Murphy J. Foster, two judges and the sheriff persuaded the crowd to disperse by promising a speedy trial, and the next morning Lovely pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty-four years in the penitentiary. Papers nationally credited Foster and treated the case as a sign of a turn against lynching.

According to the St. Mary Banner, on Sunday morning Mrs. Rene Hebert was driving a buggy to church in Franklin with her young son when a man named Esau Lovely stopped her in the cut-off about three miles above town and robbed her. She was described as the wife of a sugar planter and a daughter of A. A. Delahoussaye of Franklin. A Franklin dispatch named the accused 'Boas' and called the attack an 'attempted assault', while a New Orleans dispatch called him an ex-convict, alias 'Possum', who had confessed.

Her relatives, the sheriff's deputies and a crowd of citizens hunted for the accused man. Sheriff Sanders caught him, reportedly as he was making for the swamps, and had him in jail before the crowd learned of the arrest.

That night a crowd gathered at the jail, put at about 250 by the Banner, 200 by the Franklin dispatch and 400 by New Orleans correspondents. Foster, Judges A. C. Allen and H. D. Smith, Sheriff Sanders and District Attorney W. K. Wilson told the crowd that the prisoner would be tried at once if the law were allowed to take its course. New Orleans dispatches said Foster spoke from a jail window and begged the men not to stain the state's history with another lynching, after which the crowd went home.

At about 10:30 the next morning, at a special term of court, Lovely pleaded guilty and received thirty-four years at hard labor, which the Banner called 'the full limit of the law'. He was moved for safety and sent to Baton Rouge on the first train, less than 48 hours after the robbery. On July 22 the parish grand jury praised the judge, sheriff and district attorney for disposing of 'the highway robber, Esau Lovely' and commended the crowd's patience, saying the provocation had been great. No report of any charge against members of the crowd was found.

New Orleans dispatches carried the story on July 14 to the New York Sun, the Washington Post, the St. Louis Republic and the Minneapolis Journal, and reprints followed from Pennsylvania to Arkansas. These reports centered on Foster rather than on Lovely, under headlines such as 'Mob Persuaded to Leave' and 'Senator Stopped Lynching'. The Washington Evening Star argued that officials who upheld the law lacked no courage, and Maine papers quoting the Boston Transcript set Foster against Senator Tillman.

Louisiana papers read the case differently. The St. Mary Banner, under the headline 'Swift Justice', said a guilty plea within 48 hours was 'the only method to be followed in all such cases', and in August again held up Judge Allen's handling as a model. The Lafayette Advertiser's subhead called Lovely 'An Intending Negro Ravisher' even though he pleaded guilty only to robbery, and the St. Martinville Weekly Messenger argued that a Black man who assaulted a woman 'will and should be lynched'.
In the Black press the case appeared only in a Colored American editorial, 'Daylight Ahead', which listed Foster's stand, without names or place, among signs that the 'lynching habit' was waning.

Accounts differ on the charge: the local Banner, the grand jury and the Lafayette Advertiser describe a robbery, while the out-of-town dispatches call it an attempted assault. They also differ on what the crowd did, since New Orleans dispatches say its leaders demanded the jail keys at midnight, while the Banner, published in Franklin, says no move was made to capture the prisoner. The Franklin dispatch filed that night reported the crowd already dispersing at 10 o'clock.

bases: A crowd of 200 to 400 gathered at the St. Mary parish jail to lynch a jailed Black prisoner and dispersed after officials promised a speedy trial (A1, A5, A13).
No one was killed: the crowd that came to lynch Lovely dispersed, and he was sentenced in court the next day (A1, A13); the episode is a threatened or attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The local St. Mary Banner (A13), the New Orleans wire (A1, A5, A7) and a separate Franklin dispatch (A9) independently report the crowd at the jail and its dispersal, though they differ on whether the crowd made any move on the jail.

accounts.label: Local paper (St. Mary Banner)
accounts.gist: A crowd of about 250 gathered near the jail, 'no doubt' to lynch the prisoner, but made no move to take him and dispersed on the officials' assurance of a speedy trial.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: A mob of several hundred or 400 went to the jail at midnight to lynch the prisoner, demanded the keys, and was turned back by Senator Foster's appeal from the jail window.

accounts.label: Franklin dispatch of July 12
accounts.gist: A negro named 'Boas', armed with a rope and an iron pipe, attempted an assault; a mob of 200 gathered and was dispersing at 10 o'clock after Foster and Judge Smith spoke.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Colored American counted Foster's stand against a lynching attempt among signs that the 'lynching habit' was turning.

framing.detail: The Evening Star editorial ('Standing Up for the Law') and Boston Transcript comment praised Foster and the officials and condemned lynching, contrasting Foster with Tillman.
The local St. Mary Banner headlined 'Swift Justice' and the grand jury called the provocation great, praising speedy punishment rather than condemning the crowd.
The St. Martinville Weekly Messenger said a negro who assaults a woman 'will and should be lynched' and blamed the 'negro brute' for any lynching.
The Lafayette Advertiser headlined 'A Lynching Averted' with the subhead 'An Intending Negro Ravisher Left to the Law' although the plea was to robbery.
The Colored American's 'Daylight Ahead' praised Foster's opposition to the lynching attempt while urging Black ministers and teachers to preach morality.

conflicts.note: The local Banner and the Sun agree on Lovely; 'Boas' appears only in the early Franklin dispatch.
The local paper and grand jury describe robbery, and the Lafayette Advertiser says the plea was to robbery; the attempted-assault charge appears in the out-of-town dispatches.
